items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation: government response
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Ministerial foreword; paragraphs 12, 15, 17 and 76; section 5.1.2 (central function, horizon scanning)
items.quote: The challenges posed by AI will ultimately require legislative action in every country once understanding of risk has matured.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. The last full statement of the UK framework: five principles applied by existing regulators, no new statute for now, a central function in government for risk monitoring and horizon scanning, and regulators asked to publish their approaches by 30 April 2024. Published by the previous government; the page was last updated 6 February 2024.

items.title: The King's Speech 2024
items.locator: Paragraph following the Employment Rights Bill
items.quote: seek to establish the appropriate legislation to place requirements on those working to develop the most powerful artificial intelligence models
items.why: The present government's stated intention on AI legislation, delivered 17 July 2024. It is an intention to seek legislation for developers of the most powerful models, not a named bill and not a general AI law.

items.title: The King's Speech 2026
items.locator: Whole speech searched for 'artificial intelligence' and 'AI': no occurrence. Passage quoted is the Regulating for Growth Bill
items.quote: reduce the burden of unnecessary regulation through innovation
items.why: Read in full to check the status of any UK AI bill. The speech as published, delivered 13 May 2026, does not mention artificial intelligence and names no AI bill. It names a Regulating for Growth Bill and a Digital Access to Services Bill. Parliament's bills site could not be read in this pass, so private members' bills were not checked.

items.title: Regulators' strategic approaches to AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Introductory text and the list 'Regulator updates'
items.quote: requesting an update on how they are taking forward the White Paper proposals
items.why: The index to each regulator's published approach to AI, the nearest thing to a watch list for a UK organisation. Thirteen bodies are listed, including the Bank of England, Competition and Markets Authority, Equality and Human Rights Commission, Financial Conduct Authority, Information Commissioner's Office and Ofcom. The updates date from spring 2024 and have not been refreshed on this page.

items.title: AI and the FCA: our approach
items.locator: Opening section; 'How do our current rules apply?'; page updates (last updated 2 October 2026, editorial amendment)
items.quote: We do not plan to introduce extra regulations for AI.
items.why: A sector regulator's current position, in its own words: no AI-specific rules, reliance on existing frameworks such as the Consumer Duty and the Senior Managers and Certification Regime. Shows why scanning in the UK means watching how existing rules are applied, not waiting for an AI rulebook.

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
items.locator: Opening paragraph; link to 'Our plans for new and updated guidance'
items.quote: All the provisions affecting data protection law and the Privacy and Electronic Regulations Communications are now in force.
items.why: The regulator's status page for the Act. Confirms that the data protection provisions are all in force and points to its plans page, which says planned guidance has been reprioritised and some withdrawn because of the Act. Page metadata date 12 February 2026; the statement that all provisions are in force was on the page on 2 October 2026.

items.title: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026, S.I. 2026/82
items.locator: Regulations 2 (5 February 2026, including reg. 2(j), section 80, automated decision-making), 3 (19 June 2026) and 5 (saving for decisions taken before 5 February 2026)
items.why: Source of the figure. Shows how one Act arrives in stages: this sixth set of commencement regulations brought the automated decision-making provisions into force on 5 February 2026 and the complaints provisions on 19 June 2026, with savings for decisions already taken. Original (as made) version; made 29 January 2026.

items.title: AI Act, Article 113: Entry into force and application (AI Act Service Desk copy)
items.locator: Article 113, points (a)-(d), marked AMENDED and NEW; read with the Service Desk timeline page and the Commission's 'AI Act' policy page ('Application timeline')
items.quote: 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III
items.why: The Commission's own copy of the Act, not the Official Journal: EUR-Lex returned an empty page for the amending Regulation (OJ L, 2026/1744). The Service Desk says its text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026; the page footer still names the 2024 official version, so it is not fully updated. As read: general application 2 August 2026; Annex III high-risk rules 2 December 2027; Annex I product rules 2 August 2028; Chapters I and II from 2 February 2025.

items.title: AI and Digital Hub 2024/5
items.locator: Opening statement and list of eight case studies; FAQs
items.quote: AI and Digital Hub was a one-year pilot that is now closed for queries.
items.why: The cross-regulator advice service named in the 2024 government response. It launched in April 2024 as a twelve-month pilot and is closed to new queries; eight case studies of its informal advice remain. A reminder that sources of help change as well as rules.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Provision 28 (page 13 of the document); Introduction, 'Reporting on the Code' (activities and outcomes); Principle C
items.quote: The board should explain what procedures are in place to identify and manage emerging risks.
items.why: The governance hook for horizon scanning. Boards of companies that follow the Code should assess emerging as well as principal risks and explain their procedures for identifying them, on a comply or explain basis. The Code also asks for reporting on activities and outcomes, which a change log supplies.

items.title: Regulatory Initiatives Grid - 10th Edition (May 2026)
items.publisher: Financial Conduct Authority, for the Financial Services Regulatory Initiatives Forum
items.locator: Opening paragraphs; 'Scope of the Grid'; 'Understanding how to use the Regulatory Initiatives Grid'
items.quote: The Regulatory Initiatives Grid sets out the planned regulatory initiatives for the next 24 months.
items.why: A ready-made horizon scan published by the regulators themselves. The Forum's members publish one forward calendar of planned regulatory initiatives so that firms can plan for their timing. Financial services only, and it lists initiatives of Forum members, so it will not show every AI-related change (for example EU law). First published and last updated 19 May 2026; the landing page was read, not the Grid PDF.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 6.1: Compliance
items.locator: SYSC 6.1.1R (dated 03/01/2018); SYSC 6.1.3R (compliance function to monitor and assess)
items.quote: A firm must establish, implement and maintain adequate policies and procedures sufficient to ensure compliance
items.why: The binding rule behind regulatory scanning in a regulated firm: an FCA-authorised firm must maintain policies and procedures sufficient to ensure it complies with its obligations under the regulatory system, which it cannot do without knowing when those obligations change. Sector-specific (FCA firms); the rule does not mention horizon scanning or AI, and no equivalent general duty exists for unregulated companies.

items.title: Data Use and Access Act 2025: plans for commencement
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: 'Background' (Stages 1 to 4); summaries of Stage 1 to 3 regulations. Page shows 'Published: 25 July 2025', 'Last updated: 5 February 2026'
items.quote: The government plans to commence these provisions in 4 main stages
items.why: Government's own forward timetable for the Act that changed UK automated decision-making law: four stages, with the main data protection changes about six months after Royal Assent and the complaints duty about twelve months after. The kind of pre-announced schedule a scanning process should have logged in July 2025. Last updated 5 February 2026, so it does not record the later stage; the commencement regulations on legislation.gov.uk are the authority for dates.

items.title: Our plans for new and updated guidance
items.quote: We'll update this information regularly so that you can confidently track a product as it develops.
items.why: The data protection regulator's pipeline of guidance, by stage (drafting, consultation, redrafting, withdrawn, published). Says planned guidance has been deprioritised or withdrawn because of the Data (Use and Access) Act. The topic lists load separately and were not read as raw text, so no claim is made here about any particular item or date. Undated page; the 2 October log records a metadata date of 30 June 2026.

items.title: Timeline for the Implementation of the EU AI Act
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Opening statement; entries for 02 Aug 2026, 02 Dec 2026, 02 Dec 2027 and 02 Aug 2028
items.quote: The EU's AI Act legislation applies progressively, with a full roll-out of the main application milestones foreseen by 2 August 2028.
items.why: The Commission's one-page calendar of the AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI: transparency rules and enforcement from 2 August 2026, a transitional date of 2 December 2026, Annex III high-risk rules from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product rules from 2 August 2028. A Commission summary, not the legal text; Article 113 (already on this list) is the authority. Relevant only to organisations within the Act's reach. Undated page.

items.title: UK signs first international treaty addressing risks of artificial intelligence
items.locator: Press release, body text (paragraph beginning 'Once the treaty is ratified'); list of the 3 over-arching safeguards
items.quote: Once the treaty is ratified and brought into effect in the UK, existing laws and measures will be enhanced.
items.why: An instrument for the watch list that sits outside the UK and EU statute books: the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, signed by the UK on 5 September 2024. Government said existing laws and measures would be enhanced once it is ratified and brought into effect. A press release, not the treaty text; the Council of Europe's treaty pages refused automated reading today, so whether and when the UK has ratified, and the Convention's entry into force, are not verified here.

items.title: The Futures Toolkit: tools for strategic futures for policymakers and analysts
items.locator: 'Tools at a glance' (Horizon Scanning); chapter 'Horizon scanning' under 'What is changing?'
items.quote: The systematic collection of insights on emerging trends and weak signals of change to identify potential threats, risks and opportunities.
items.why: Government's own definition of horizon scanning and a five-step method for doing it, described as looking ahead, across and around, beyond the usual timescales and sources. Written for policy officials, not for corporate regulatory tracking, and voluntary; used here for what distinguishes a scanning process from reading the news. 2024 edition; the HTML page shows 'Updated 29 August 2024'.

items.title: The Brussels Effect and Artificial Intelligence: How EU regulation will impact the global AI market
items.quote: we tentatively conclude that both de facto and de jure Brussels effects are likely for parts of the EU regulatory regime
items.why: Why a UK organisation should track EU rules even if it does not trade there. The authors argue EU AI regulation is likely to change the products offered outside the EU and to influence other jurisdictions' laws. A research report posted as a preprint, not peer reviewed; written in 2022 about the proposed Act, before its adoption and before the 2026 amendments, and its conclusions are stated as tentative.

items.title: Complying with the EU AI Act
items.publisher: Jacintha Walters, Diptish Dey, Debarati Bhaumik and Sophie Horsman (arXiv)
items.locator: Section IV.A ('Identifying Focus Areas'), PDF p.3-4; Section III (fifteen responses); Conclusion
items.quote: The overall average compliance score for all respondents and categories is 57%.
items.why: Evidence of what happens without preparation. A questionnaire scored fifteen organisations against the requirements of the then-proposed AI Act; the average score was 57%, and organisations with 1-50 employees scored lower than larger ones. Preprint, not peer reviewed here; very small, self-selected sample from 2023, mostly self-reported answers, measured against a draft of the Act. Indicative only.
